utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Mladen Naletilic and Vinko Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Well, Mr. Seric, we have received your motion dated the 27th August, 2002, in which you listed six potential witnesses that you are going to call in the following sequence and you also indicated what kind of protective measures that you are requesting from this Trial Chamber. I would like to turn to the Prosecutor to see whether there is any objections to all those six witnesses, as well as the protective measures they asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. If I might have just a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Mr. President, generally speaking we would have no objection. I would just state for the record our continuing concern about the number, the extent of the protective measures in the case and again it's not objecting to any particular one but I do think it does present overall problems for a case of this magnitude when so much of the evidence is received with such deep protective measures. Basically almost as a routine practice but I just state that as a general concern. We have no specific objections, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe that this Trial Chamber shares the view expressed by you. Yes, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with regard to the issue of protective measures, I would like to say that we will have a change, that we will advise you of in the course of the day. For witness under number 5 we are going to ask for a closed session. We have prepared a motion. It is being translated just as we speak. So we are asking for even stronger protective measures because the witness under number 5 put that as a condition to us. He has had some problems. His identity has been revealed and it has been found out that he was going to testify here. I am very concerned when the -- Mr. Scott says that he objects to -- he doesn't object to the protective measures but he expresses concern. However I would like to ask this Chamber how do our witnesses differ from the Prosecutor's witnesses, who were -- who enjoyed the maximum protective measures, who enjoyed not only the customary protective measures but also it testified in closed sessions? Before the beginning of this process we had a gentlemen's agreement between the Prosecution and the Defence and we promised to each other not to raise any concerns about protective measures. At the beginning, this gentlemen's agreement was honoured. However, to raise this issue now, when the Prosecutor's case is finished and forget what protective measures they asked for their witnesses, and now impose it on us that we should not ask for these measures, I don't deem this to be correct and I'm asking from this Chamber to help us with these protective measures, especially with the closed sessions. We did not want to raise any issues before this Trial Chamber when our witnesses complained that their identity was revealed, and we are clear that the information on the identity of the witnesses can come only from the police and the police in turn can receive that information only through the organs that check their credibility. So Mr. President, this is as far our protective measures are concerned. We are going to ask for a closed session for one witness and I'm really crossed with this Prosecutor's position regarding the protective measures we are asking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Par, you have to understand that this Trial Chamber has done its utmost to accommodate any request from both parties concerning protective measures in the past proceedings. Generally speaking, we satisfied all the requests made by both parties in this aspect. But we have to bear in mind that as the principle, the trial should be conducted in open session, and it's also the right of the accused to have a fair and open hearing before this Tribunal. So, Mr. Par, if there -- if you ask for the closed session, we are expecting your motion, the written motion, on this respect. And for the later witnesses, my advice is try to talk to your witness to relax the protective measures, at least we should have some heard in open session in the proceedings. Up to now, the five witnesses, in the least, are asking for the protective measures is granted by this Trial Chamber. As for witness number 5, we will act in response to the motion filed by the Defence counsel of Mr. Martinovic. Are you ready to call your first witness? Yes. Mr. Usher, would you please bring in the witness? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Seric. Your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: We are going to ask you to pause after my question in order to enable our interpreters to follow you properly. Maybe the best thing for you to do would be to follow the transcript on your monitor and when the black dot stops, you can start giving your answer. Can you see the dot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask the usher to show you a piece of paper with your first name and last name. Don't read it aloud, just say yes or no if the data, if the information is correct, just say yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I shall be addressing you as Witness MO. That is your pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct. Mr. President, can we go to private session? Because I'm going to ask the witness to give us some personal data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: We are now in open session, Witness, which means that you should be careful not to say anything that could reveal your identity. During the attack by the Serbian aggressor and the Yugoslav Army on Mostar, were you -- did you have any military engagement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us which unit were you a member of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, I was a member of the 3rd Battalion, but at the beginning it was Territorial Defence, and then it was the 3rd Battalion and I was there for ten to 15 days, and then we set up a sabotage platoon, an independent platoon, and I was a member of that platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in that last unit, in the independent sabotage platoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Until the spring.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Of what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, did you know Mr. Vinko Martinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Where did you get to know him and when did you meet him? For how long did you know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I knew him from school, from elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you go to the same class?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes. For four years we were classmates.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: The first four years?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: The first four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Please can you make a pause and let me finish my question? Do you know what was Martinovic's job? What did he do, especially before the war, before 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I used to see him driving a taxi.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something more specifically? What did that mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I saw him driving a taxi. I saw him being a taxi driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: After the beginning of the war, that is of the conflict between the Serbian Army and the JNA and their aggression against Mostar, do you know what Vinko Martinovic did at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Vinko Martinovic was a HOS commander, the commander of HOS for Mostar, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What do you know about that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I know that they manned the line on Tito's Bridge. This is where I used to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the members of that unit were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I knew some of the members of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know the national composition of the members of that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes. It was composed of all the three ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, can you tell us which ethnic groups are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: There were Croats, Muslims and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the day, that is if you still remember it, of the 9th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us what happened, what went on, that day? And I mean only what you personally saw, heard or experienced.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: On the eve of that, with a friend called Pehar, a went to a flat and sometime in the morning, gunfire started from all four sides, and that is all that I know about that particular day. I never left the flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in your friend's apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I was there several days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Then I moved to my brother-in-law's at Rudnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And after that, did you join a unit? If you did, which one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: After that, some friends came up to invite me, and I joined the Benko Penavic unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Could you roughly fix the time when that happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Well, it could have been about 20 days after the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you have any problems in that unit? And if you did, why did you have them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Well, nobody attacked me, nobody assaulted me, but several times I heard from behind my back, "Look at this balija." So that was my problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us all, and especially the Court, why did that happen? Why would they call you that? Why do they talk behind your back about you? What do you call yourself? What is you are ethnic group? So tell us, what do you say? What are you? What is you are ethnic group? What is your religion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I call myself a Croat and my religion is Islamic. So I suppose that is the reason, because this is an offensive name for ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Finish your answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: It's a pejorative name for Croats of Islamic faith and Muslims, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what do people around you consider you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: That I'm a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you leave that unit, Benko Penavic, eventually? And what did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I left -- or rather I was thrown out of the unit. And then I joined Stela's unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when was that? When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: It was after their joint action, when they attacked Hum and that Hrvoje house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you remember roughly at least when that happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I believe it was late September.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: You said that Vinko Martinovic admitted you in his unit. Did he know that you were of Islamic faith?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes, of course he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you then suffer because of that? Did he cause you any problems, he or one of his soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No. Quite the reverse. I was on good terms with everybody, and with him in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you ever feel being harassed or being looked askance because you were of Islamic faith?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No. I was even helped.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what did you do in the Vinko Skrobo unit? That is, what was your specific duty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I held the line on the Bulevar, and that was my only duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which part of the front line did you hold on the Bulevar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: The health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: On the basis of assignments given you, can you tell us if you were responsible for the depth of the area behind that part of the front line that you held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you take shifts on the front line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: How many of you, how many members of the unit were in a shift? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Well, perhaps 15 men each shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: How long were the shifts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: 12 hours, sometimes eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And when the shift would be over, regardless of the exact time, whether it was in daytime or at night-time, what did you do? Where did you go after you finished your shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Well, I went where I wanted to. Sometimes I'd go to the base. Sometimes I'd go and have lunch. Sometimes I'd go straight home. Or perhaps to some coffee bar. There was no order as to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you have to notify anyone about your movements after the completion of a shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No, of course not. Nobody had to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did your commander, Vinko Martinovic, know what you did after you had done your shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No. There was no way he could know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: After the shift, would you keep your uniform on or would you change?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I would keep my uniform on because I didn't have any civilian clothes. All that had stayed behind on the Bulevar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And did you see any of the members of your unit during that leisure time or when you socialised? Did you meet with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what kind of clothes would they have, as a rule?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Well, uniforms, as likely as not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: As a unit, did you go to other parts of the town in an organised manner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you personally, on your own or with your friends from the unit, go around the town, go with your friends?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: At times. Sometimes yes, sometimes no. One or two perhaps. But I had a number of friends around. I did not need to walk around with anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know which units held that front line apart from you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Well, some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: We shall now show you a photograph, that is an air photograph, of this part of the Bulevar, 14.5. I have a copy with me. Or perhaps the Registrar will -- no. I think it will be faster this way. Let's have it on the ELMO so that everybody can see what we are talking about. Witness, now, will you take the marker and make a circle, first the segment of the front line that you tell us you held next to the health centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And put number 1, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Now tell us what you've just told us, that you knew some of the units that manned the front line next to you. To the left here on the photograph, who was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Here, to the left, was Benko Penavic. Should I mark it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Yes, do, and put number 2 there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was to the right of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No. I don't think that those guys were from --

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: The photograph can stay there because we'll need it still. Can you tell us how strong was the unit at the time when you were with it? I mean Vinko Skrobo unit. How strong was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Well, it could have been 60 men, 70 on the -- at the outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you stay with the unit until it was disbanded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: If you remember, can you tell us some of the men who were most frequently with you on a shift? If you do remember their names we will go into private session. If you don't then tell us so.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes. I remember some of the men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: This individual that you tell us commanded your shift, did he keep this duty all the time, all the time that you were with the Vinko Skrobo ATG?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in so far as you can remember, whether Vinko Martinovic had a rank, any rank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: He didn't have any patches and I'm not aware of any rank that he might have had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: How did you and other members of the unit, as you could hear them, how did you address him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Well, I addressed him as Stela or Puki or Skolski and those others addressed him as Stela or Puki.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Would you mind telling us what this Puki means?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Well, something like short for colonel, an endearment for colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know which larger unit did your unit, that is Vinko Skrobo ATG belong to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge whatsoever, that is whether you heard or saw, where did your unit receive its orders from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I do not know that but possibly from the town command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you describe to us one of your run-of-the-mill days in your shift, in the unit, from the moment that you would arrive and how did you spend that particular day, any day? How were you made responsible for something? In what way? And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: We had three bunkers and then we took shifts there. And we were -- when we were not at the bunkers, we were over there drinking tea or coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what do you call a bunker? What was it really?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Well, those were some wooden boards and sacks piled up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Piled up where? I mean physically where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: In this building. At the windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Which building, tell us for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Do you want me to show you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Yes, point at it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: No, you have to do it on the ELMO so that we can see it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: [indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what building is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: This is the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Were you -- were there any fortifications next to the health centre building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Were there any hurdles, any obstacles around it, on the Liska Street, on the Bulevar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what kind of obstacles, barriers, and where were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Across the road, there were sacks piled up, and there was a cord with some blankets or some sheets of cloth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Will you draw a line where that was and put a number 2 next to that line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: [indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we already have number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, yes, indeed, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Put number 3, sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Were there any other barriers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes. At the junction here, at the cross roads. Those crosses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Will you please put letter X there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: If there were a number of them, then put some more X's there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yeah, but I can't remember. Not more than two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And put number 4 next to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us what was the purpose of it all, of these crosses, sand bags, this cord with blankets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: The sand bags served to save us from getting killed, to take shelter behind them, at this position, position number 1. And those behind where we had this sheet of cloth, it was there so that nobody would get killed when we went to the front line, because some people did get killed there, and wounded. And these crosses -- the purpose of these crosses was because once I'm sure they sent a car bomb against us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: These crosses, did they preclude any traffic up or down the Liska Street in either direction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Why, yes, because -- because that car bomb had passed through unimpeded when they sent it, and then it prevented this car bomb to move on further and reach us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: According to your recollection of that time, when you were on the Bulevar, or before that, while you were with the Benko Penavic ATG, was there daily fighting there on the front line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No, no, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you know, and I'm referring to the period of time when you were with the Vinko Skrobo ATG, did you know who manned the front line on the opposite, on the -- across the street on the opposite side of the Bulevar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Well, we didn't always know that, but at times there were some guys from Mostar and we called out to them and we talked, we knew their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What would you call out to them and what did you talk about with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Oh, well, joking, asking them, "What are you doing?" Or whether somebody had any trouble with -- whether somebody needed help, whether somebody needed to be taken across if he wanted to cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Would you at times also agree a ceasefire, to stop the fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes, several times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we cannot keep up with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour, Judge Diarra, I'll try to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when was that, on what occasions would you agree a ceasefire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: It happened on those occasions when somebody needed to cross over. I mean a civilian, somebody from our side to their side or the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge of such a case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I used to see people crossing, and my mother crossed from over there in that same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you now tell us about your personal example, that is when your mother crossed? Could you describe it for us? When and how was it organised, from which to which side did your mother cross?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: My mother crossed from the left bank, and it was all arranged by Dubi. How, I don't know, but she crossed over here where the 4th Battalion held the positions next to Roko's Bakery.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us what ethnic group does your mother belong to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: My mother is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Whilst you were with the Vinko Skrobo unit or later, did you hear anyone impersonate himself as a member of your unit, say that he's a Stelici, Stela's boy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what was that all about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Well, whatever kind of wrong thing was done, people would say, Stela's boys, Stelici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you hear or see Vinko Martinovic's reaction to such things that happened in his name and in the name of your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I saw him see red about that once. He was very angry. And he said if he caught any one of our guys do something like that, he'd beat him well and good.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did -- and I'm -- did prisoners come or were prisoners brought to your Vinko Skrobo ATG?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were brought there but I found them there. They slept there. I remember some prisoners who slept there and worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us where did they sleep? How was that arranged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: They slept in our base on Kalemova, and there were two more guys here on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Where were those two guys? Where on the front line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Where we had coffee. We called it Trica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you point at the place on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes, I can. [indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And will you put another circle and put number 5 so that we know what you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Were they exposed to gunfire there or the action of whatever type of weapon from the other side of the front line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No. That is where we slept, had our coffee or tea, so the ground floor, or rather not the ground floor. It's in a basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you -- could you see how did they get to the base, the prisoners, I mean.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No. I didn't. I saw them -- I would see them walk around there or doing something with cars, but they could -- they moved around freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And how did these two prisoners find themselves at the position that you marked with number 5?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Well, like we did. They walked from the base on their own, freely, and down to the front line and back. Nobody escorted them. They of course had to look out not to be hit by a bullet, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And did you and they were likewise protected when coming to and going from that site that you marked with number 5? I mean against direct fire from the other side of the front line.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes. We were protected by bags and there was this canvass, this sheet of cloth so they couldn't see us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you come to know any one of those prisoners? Did you talk with them and thus come to know them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I knew both of them. One of them I came to know of. Later on he worked with me in this entertainment hall. The other one's name, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: You said that they were doing something with cars. Can you it tell us what is it that they did, from what you could see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: They did something with the cars. They repaired them. I had a car and Redzo would repair some things on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What do you mean they repaired or reinforced the cars? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: They would put some plates so as to prevent anybody from getting killed in the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: The prisoners, and particularly these two that you saw more often, tell us did they stay in that position of their own will? Were they under any threat? Were there any guards around them? Were they held at gunpoint? Can you tell us something about their actions, about their stay in that area? What did they actually do there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: They would make cups of coffee, cups of tea. They slept just like we did, with the only difference between that we went to the bunker. Nobody guarded them. They moved around freely. They talked to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What was their food like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Whatever we had to eat, they had to eat. When it was cans, it was cans. When we had lunch, they had lunch. Each and every one of them on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Where did you have lunch?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: We would go to the Hladovina in Zdenko Zubac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you see any of them engaged in very hard physical labour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No. I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: On your segment of the line, in front of the health centre or around that building, were there any trenches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: We've heard in this courtroom that some people were engaged in hard, physical labour, like digging trenches around the health centre. Was the situation always the same as it is now on the photo with regards to the alleged trenches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I must say I never saw them. I must say that it looks nicer now than it did then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: The prisoners who worked, who did all sorts of menial tasks for the unit, did they receive any remuneration for their work? Were they compensated for their work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I don't think that they did receive any money. They did receive food and drinks. As far as I know, they did not get any money. They shared their meals with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What about cigarettes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes, they did receive cigarettes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you notice fear or pressure or that they were afraid of the soldiers, of you personally, of Vinko Martinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I did not talk to them a lot but I spoke to Redzo. Redzo was having a good time actually. He didn't want to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: From what you could see, while you were holding this part of the front line, did any of the prisoners work on the Bulevar itself, in front of the health centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No. I never saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know somebody called Nenad Harmandzic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes, I know the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What do you know about that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: He was an acquaintance before the war. He was a policeman. He was a tall guy, a strongly built guy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: How -- what was his height? How tall was he? What would you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: He was much taller than me. He may have been 2 metres high.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What do you know about what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: After the war, I heard that he had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of a person called Halil Ajanic, also known as Lopata?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him from before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you see that person as one of the prisoners in the Vinko Skrobo unit working there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No. I saw him in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: When did you see him in town? Was that during the conflict between the BH Army and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: While I was with the Benko Penavic, I would see him there. He had two children. They lived in Avenija across from the Projektant building. That is where he lived, in an apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the date 17 September, 1993, when there was a somewhat stronger conflict between the BH Army and the HVO? You were then with the Benko Penavic ATG you said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you were at the time during that operation on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I was in a trench between the positions of the 4th Battalion and Aleksic House.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you maybe see that position in this photo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No. It is a bit further from the last house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Where in the photo, on the right-hand side or on the left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: On the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you hear or see a tank being used in the course of that operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I heard that there was a tank in that operation. I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you hear the sound coming from that tank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes. I believe two shells were fired from it. I can't remember that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: On that day, did you see any of the prisoners attached to either the Benko Penavic ATG or the Vinko Skrobo ATG?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I did not see them in the Benko Penavic, but from my position, I couldn't see the positions of the Vinko Skrobo ATG.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you received monthly remuneration while you were a member of the Vinko Skrobo ATG?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: How was that paid and who by?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: We would receive it from a clerk. I think it was Zeljo Colak or Garo. Sometimes I would get it from Dubi or one of the colleagues. Sometimes I would receive it in the coffee bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the money came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Where did you get your weapons and ammunition from? And how was that done?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: We received our weapons and ammunition in the base, Zeljo or Garo would give it to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you have enough ammunition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: We are talking about food, and you mentioned the Hladovina restaurant. What was the food like in the Hladovina restaurant and how come that the prisoners ate together with you in that same restaurant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: The food was good. We would come at our own time -- chosen time. We had an allocated slot of three hours for lunch, between 1.00 and 4.00 in the afternoon. There were tables, and we would help ourselves to as much food as we wanted to have. And the food was good.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Were there any differences between you and the prisoners in terms of the food, in terms of its quantity and quality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No. We helped ourselves to the same food, and to as much as we wanted. We helped ourselves. It was self-service.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you personally know anything about the attitude of Vinko Martinovic towards Muslims? Did he help Muslims in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I know he was on very good terms with Redzo, that he was on very good terms with Benac and helped him, and as far as I'm concerned, he was very good to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: While you were a member of the unit, did you ever see Vinko Martinovic harassing anybody? I don't mean just prisoners but also soldiers, civilians, and prisoners as well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anybody among your colleagues talking about Vinko Martinovic harassing anybody, either them or prisoners or civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you hear or read or learn in any other way why Vinko Martinovic is appearing before this Tribunal? What is he charged with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes. I've been told that he is charged with harassment and killings and overdoing in his actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know that both you and your unit are incriminated by that indictment, that everybody is charged with the same thing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question is pure speculation, nobody is charged here, I mean the units, of any crimes before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I quite agree with you. In accordance with the rules of -- this Tribunal only has jurisdiction over the person, not organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept that, Mr. President. I have finished my examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's time for a break. We will resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examination, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct that you stayed with the 3rd Battalion for a short period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And at some point, you created so-called independent sabotage platoon. Could you explain to the Trial Chamber what kind of unit was it? Why it was called independent and sabotage platoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Independent, maybe because it was Dragan Slezak, the brother of Diko Slezak. He was the guy in Mostar who was independent, who wouldn't be ordered about, and sabotage maybe because we were engaged in various operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And do you know to whom that unit, sabotage platoon, was subordinate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I don't know. We only received orders from Dragan Slezak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And who was your immediate commander in that Sabotage Unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: It was Dila.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you remember his full name? I suggest that Dila should be a sort of nickname.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: His last name was Dilic and I don't know his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Was he a Croat or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Was that unit involved in any anti-Serb or anti-Muslim operations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: That unit participated in some operations against Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, on the 9th of May, you were in town, Mostar, in the town of Mostar, but at some point, you went to one of your acquaintances and stayed in his apartment for some period of time; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I apologise. I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. I will rephrase my question. By the 9th of May, 1993, were you still a member of that sabotage unit? Did it exist at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No. It was disbanded before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: So at some point, you became a member of Benko Penavic unit. Who proposed to you become a member of that unit, and what -- okay. Who proposed you to become a member of that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: A friend of mine, Buli Prce came. They are the guys from the former sabotage platoon, asked me if I would join them, and I said yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you know at that time that Benko Penavic unit was predominantly a Croat unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No. I didn't know that. We didn't join that unit. That is what I discussed with my friends. We went straight to the front line. I didn't know the composition of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And who was in command of that unit, Benko Penavic unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: It was Baja.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: You knew him before the war; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did he talk to you before admitting you into his unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did anyone from the command structure of this unit talk to you and briefed you on your tasks, on your position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No. Buli asked me if I wanted to join that unit. That is my colleague from the former sabotage platoon. And after that, I did not talk to anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Is it correct that Benko Penavic consisted of two -- at least two groups of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I apologise. What do you mean when you say "two groups of soldiers"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I mean that any unit is divided into platoons and other structures. How many platoons or other structures did your unit have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: We were not split into platoons, as far as I know. Maybe 50 to 60 men. But I don't know for a fact. I think 40 to 50 men. But I don't know that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And did all 40 or 50 soldiers participate in military operations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Now that you ask me, I believe they didn't. There are also some clerical staff, the guys who remained in the base all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And who was your shift commander? Or squad commander within Benko Penavic unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: At the beginning, it was Buli. He was the one we turned to, until they left the unit. When we moved to the Bulevar, to hold the line there, then it was Lola Kopilas.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know a man whose name was -- kid name was Vina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I know a guy whose name was Vina but he was not a member of our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: To which unit did he belong?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I believe he was a member of the 4th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, were you the only Muslim in Benko Penavic unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Approximately how many Muslims were there within the unit in the period when you joined it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Maybe six or seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And did all of them have similar problems like you, as being a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I don't know. None of them spoke to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you know anyone personally? I mean these Muslim soldiers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps we should go into a private session for some minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, I suggest you should remember many names of your soldier mates within Vinko Skrobo unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I remember some.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Some I never met.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you remember if there were foreign soldiers within that unit? Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 15047 to 15057.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I don't know. There were no foreign soldiers in our group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And who was your group commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: It was Dubi.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit 745.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, again I will ask you: Did you have a certificate of membership of Vinko Martinovic unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: You never had it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would like you to take a look at this document. Witness, is it correct that at least in August, 1993, the unit bore the name of Vinko Skrobo ATG?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And what was the initial name of that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Stelici or what, I don't know. Mrmak perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What the word "Mrmak" means?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't there when it was called that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And Witness, I would like you to take a look at this document again and tell me whose name you see just at the bottom of the page, as the unit's commander.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Vinko Martinovic, Stela.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Stela. Do you see his signature in this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: So this signature belongs to Mr. Vinko Martinovic; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Anybody could have signed this. I don't know his handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: You never saw any documents signed by him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And when did you leave Vinko Martinovic unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: When the war stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: But is it correct that for a short period of time, for a short period of time, prisoners still were taken from Heliodrom to some construction sites and to other places in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: When did you leave the unit? I would like to you tell me more or less precise date, at least month.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: It was in 1994, when the war stopped. Was it in April or in May?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: So it was somewhere in April or in May, 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, my cross-examination is over. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few questions, Your Honour. The Prosecution has not used the Exhibit P704 in the cross-examination. So I will not have any questions. I prepared my questions with regards to that exhibit. However, the Prosecutor did not use that exhibit so I don't have any questions. Thank you. I apologise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Questions from Judges? Judge Clark?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Witness MO, I appreciate the response which you gave to the Prosecutor that you never had a certificate of membership of the Vinko Skrobo or the Benko Penavic unit. But did you not have an ID card which permitted to you move around the town of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: Yes. I did have a military ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And did that have a photograph on it and the unit to which you belonged indicated on the ID?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: There was a code, a number. I can't remember what that was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I ask you, Witness MO, when you moved from Benko Penavic to Vinko Skrobo, was your ID card altered in any way to indicate that you were with a different unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: This ID was taken away from me in the Benko Penavic. I never asked for a new one, a replacement one, and after that I never wore or had an ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: How did you pass through any security checks without an ID?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: We did not have any security checks there. I would go to the confrontation line. From there I would go either home or to a coffee bar or to the base. Everybody knew me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And is it your evidence that throughout the town of Mostar, there were no checkpoints with -- manned by military police or home guard or anything like that, nobody check being the movements of anybody throughout the town of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MO
utterances.text: There were no barricades and I could move freely, all the way up to the Rondo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judges's questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming here to give your testimony. When the usher pulls down the blinds, he will show you out of the room. We all wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage, are there any documents to tender? Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to tender exhibits, the paper with the pseudonym, D2/41, the map of the city that the witness marked, that's D2/42, and the photo on which the witness also made markings, that's D2/43.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I have no objections and I also would like to tender one document, P745.2, P745.2. I actually used two exhibits during my cross-examination but the second one has been already admitted into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. So the documents tendered by the Defence counsel are admitted into evidence. As for the document P745.2, in your submissions, it's indicated that this document has already been tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, it has been tendered quite lately, and there was a last bunch of documents somewhere in the end of the binder and that last bunch of documents was denied, and little by little, we returned it. Some of those documents. This document belongs to the same bundle of documents which was denied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are there any objections, Mr. Seric to this particular document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have objections, Your Honour. We objected to both of these binders that the Prosecution is tendering -- are tendering little by little. We are objecting to P745.2 because the document refers to the period which is not incriminated in the indictment. So that is the simple reason for which we object to this document, this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think this Trial Chamber has made a decision concerning that bundle of documents tendered by the Prosecution. We rejected that bundle of documents into evidence just because of its late submission not because of its substance. As for this document, are those documents was issued in April, 1994, but it's related to what happened a year before. So on this consideration, this document is admitted into the evidence. It is so decided. Mr. Seric, are there any witnesses waiting outside?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there are, and Mr. Par, my colleague, Mr. Par, will examine that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have the next witness, Mr. Usher?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good afternoon. Before we start talking to you, I'm going to give you a piece of paper with your name, since the Honourable Court has granted you protective measures, your name is never going to be mentioned during this hearing. Can you please take a look at this piece of paper? And if this is indeed your name, just say yes without reading your name? After that you will be given a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Witness, in the first part of your conversation, I'm going to ask you some questions that may reveal your identity. That's why we shall move to private session. I will kindly ask Their Honours to allow us to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Witness, let's start with the period of time during the Serbian aggression against Mostar. Can you tell us where you lived at the time? Did you have any military engagements? Can you tell us something from your point of view about the period of the Serbian aggression against Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: At the beginning of the Serbian aggression, I was in Croatia working for a construction company. When the Serbian aggression started, I decided to enlist. A friend of mine took me there. He told me he would take me to a good, genuine unit. That was his expression, the way he put it. I didn't know what that meant, what the term "genuine unit" meant. He then took me to a place called Ljubuski, then he introduced me to a gentleman called Blaz Kraljevic who told me he was the commander of that unit. That's how I decided to join that unit, whose name was HOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So it was a HOS unit in Ljubuski, whose commander was Blaz Kraljevic. What were the tasks of that unit? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I was with the headquarters, with the staff, and I was engaged in the security for several months.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Several months, you're saying. Does that mean that after that you left that unit and joined some other unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I heard that a war had broken out in Mostar. Mostar had already been occupied by the Serbian reservists. However the open conflict started in April, 1992, and I volunteered to go there, even if it had to be on my own, to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So you wanted to be active in Mostar? You didn't want to stay in Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Yes, I wanted to go to Mostar. It was my native town. My parents were there. They gave me a rifle, a car loaded with ammunition, and I entered the city, which was encircled and then I was told to go and report to somebody called Vinko Martinovic, Stela. I didn't know him until then. That was the first time I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: That's what were you told, and that's what you did. You are now in Mostar and did you find Stela? Did he accept you in the unit? What did you tell him? Can you tell us what the situation was like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I didn't find him on the first day. I found him on the following day. I met him deputy who then introduced me to Mr. Martinovic. It was a unit composed of volunteers. It did not have a formal military structure. It was more like a group of guys from the same street, a group of lads, friends, from the same neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: For our interpreters, can you please slow down? So when was that? What month was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: It was the end of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And now let's see, when you say that this was not a well-organised unit, that it did not have a formal structure, how strong was that unit, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: At the beginning, some 30 or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the ethnic composition of that unit was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: There were mostly Croats and Muslims in the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: What was their ratio, the ratio of Croats versus Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Half-half, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: What were the tasks of that unit? What were its assignments?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: At the beginning, we just manned a front line facing the enemy. That was at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And later on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: In June, we received an order to launch an attack across the river. The enemy was on the left bank. And we won a huge victory. It was a huge victory. There was a conflict with a Serbian paramilitary unit called Bijeli Orlovi, White Eagles. It was a huge victory. One of our guys got killed, and I was injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: That huge victory, was that the liberation of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Yes. It meant the liberation of Mostar from the Serbian aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So your unit, your HOS unit, do you believe that it was one of the units which played an important role?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Yes. An important role because before that, nobody knew about us. After that, everybody knew about us, especially about Mr. Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: You said that you were injured in that operation. What were the injuries that you sustained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: It was a gunshot wound in one of the legs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: After that, Mostar was liberated, your unit became well-known. Did you remain with the unit after you were injured? What happened with you after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: When I got better, some seven or eight days later, the first thing I wanted to do was to see my house on the left bank, and when I arrived home, the first thing I saw was that -- a group of Muslims who were looting my property, stealing things from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And now, how do you know they were Muslims? And what did you do? Please, slowly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: They were my neighbours who had some refugees from Eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina -- Herzegovina with them. And that's how I knew them. They just wanted to help themselves to my things.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: What happened? Did you prevent them? Could you prevent them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I made a deal with them. I told them I wouldn't create any problems. I told them that they could hold on to those things and when I found a lorry, a truck, I would return and transport those things to a safer place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Was the house empty at the time? Where were your parents at the time? Who lived in the house before that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: The house was empty. It was slightly damaged. There was a leak in the roof so we couldn't live in the house. There was a hole in the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: When we are talking about your house, what happened to it eventually? You told us that it was set on fire. How did that happen and when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: There were a lot of refugees, especially Muslims from Eastern Herzegovina. There were a lot of them, and since there was no well-structured government in the city, there were frequent skirmishes and incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So when we are talking about the city and about your house, you're referring to the entire city of Mostar or just the part of the city where your house was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: There were refugees all over the place and my house is in the eastern part. I remember well the date. It was the 6th of May, 1993, when my house was set on fire. That was before the breakout of conflicts with the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So that was a few days before the beginning of the conflict with Muslims. Why was it set on fire? Why would anybody do it? Did you have any information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: One of the reasons may have been that I was -- that I'm a Croat. I don't know why, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Who informed you that your house had been set on fire or did you just go there and saw it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: My Muslim neighbours informed me, so I'm not making any generalisations, the people of all kinds, and those people who told me, who informed me, were really feeling very embarrassed for having to tell me that some other Muslims had done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Just one more question before you break, if you'll allow me, Your Honours. So that all happened a few days before the breakout of an open conflict between Croats and Muslims. Did you, before, have any problems being a Croat in the eastern part of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Some ten days or 15 days before the open conflict, I was passing by the old bridge, and there was a checkpoint manned by the BH Army. They harassed me there. It was a close shave. I did not suffer any consequences. But it was just a close shave. After that, I decided not to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So when you say harassment, did that have anything to do with your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I believe so, because it was the Muslim refugees from Eastern Herzegovina who harassed me. Maybe the local Muslims would not have done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that it would be advisable for us to have a break now, and then I would like to continue after the break, if I may suggest that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Witness, I was asked by the interpreters to try to slow down even more. So let us do our best to take it easy, and I will show you when you are to start your answer, because there is a problem. We speak over each other, and then it is difficult to keep up. Right. We were talking about a period which preceded immediately the conflict between the Croats and the Muslims. The events on the eve of the 9th of May, 1993. Tell us, during that period, that is on the eve of this conflict, were you militarily engaged anywhere? And if yes, tell us where.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I was engaged in the 2nd HVO Brigade. It's called Pionirska Engineers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: But did we hear how is it that you turned up in this new unit? You told us after the victory with HOS and after the liberation of Mostar, that was your -- the unit that you were with. Now, how did it come about that you joined this new unit on the eve of the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: When the war with the Serbs ended, I thought that that was the end of war as such. And I went back to my place of work in Croatia. However, the situation began to become more complicated with time, some incidents happened, an incident here, an incident there, so that I'd say sometime in March, 1993, I was called up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So the unit that you now joined was the unit to which you were mobilised. On the 9th of May, 1993, were you in that unit and what happened to you then? Describe to us briefly that 9th of May, from your point of view.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: On the 9th of May, 1993, I was with that HVO unit, and then an all-out conflict in the town broke out. I was in the barracks. We were not involved in any combat, those of us who were in the barracks. We merely guarded the barracks in case it was attacked by Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So that 9th of May you spent in the barracks and after that, what? After the 9th of May, did you stay with that unit or did you join in, the war had already started, what happened to you then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I wasn't with that unit long. A friend -- I came across a friend, a friend whom I knew from the HOS and he said that our former commander from the HOS, that is Vinko Martinovic, Stela, was about to put together a unit made of those guys who had been in the HOS. And I accepted it wholeheartedly because I knew Stela as a good combatant from the war against the Serbs, and I respected him. The HVO was not ready for that war. They simply were not ready and we needed men like Stela. So I couldn't wait for that. For the last money that I had, I bought a rifle and went to Stela.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now you'll tell us when was that approximately, the date, how many days after the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I can't really tell you the exact date but it could have been the end of May or early June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And why did you buy your rifle? Isn't it that you go and join a unit and their rifles and uniforms and all the rest of the soldier's gear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Well, let's talk plain language. I was with the HVO and I was with this regular unit but I was disenchanted. I did not see them as some organised formation that would really be up to fight. And that was the only reason. And I knew that Stela was capable and that he respected us. I mean he knew how to treat men. That was the reason. And I preferred to buy it for my own money but to be with the right people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. So now we've come to Stela's unit, so it's late May or you don't know, early June, 1993, you're not sure. You come to the unit. How do you become a member of that unit and what is the situation like then? What kind of a unit is it? Tell us first, are you admitted, are you put on record? What did it look like? You reported there. What did it look like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Well, we'd agreed to meet in a tavern that belonged to a man called Pero so this good friend of mine and I met there. In the beginning, there were no official premises so we met in this tavern and I talked with Stela, of course he knew that he was a good fighter from the HOS. He was happy to see me. He knew that I'd been wounded and that was how I was taken on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: How strong was that unit at that time? How many men were there, roughly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Well, 30 odd perhaps. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you know those men? Who were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I knew them because they were with the HOS, yes, I knew them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: And some of them I knew from around town.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Were they people who perhaps lived in that part of the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Yes, by and large, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And where were the positions of that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: We spent the whole war holding the line next to the health centre, from the beginning to the end, at least while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And what was the unit called?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: In the beginning, we were called Mrmak. I didn't even know what that was until later on that somebody told us that it was Stela's dog's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: At that time, in that unit, was there a formal chain of command, to call it that? Who was the commander? How was this unit structured at the time when you joined it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Well, the unit was divided into four groups. Our commander was Stela. But there was no strict military organisation. We simply knew one another. We were friends. I perceived Stela as a friend rather than as a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So we are talking about this first -- about this early period, this May. Did you get logistics from somewhere? Any salaries? Armament, assignments?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Well we began to get our salaries later on. I had my own rifle so I didn't need another one but the salaries began to arrive later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And how long did you stay with that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Some five months perhaps, maybe six. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now, my question, with regard to this first period, May, and then during those five or six months, what changes took place in the unit? And I'll have some questions about that. That is, did the assignments of that unit change in relation to what was in the beginning over those five -- over that period of five or six months?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: As far as I know, they didn't. We always manned that segment of the front line next to the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did the unit ever move to another position? Did it ever leave the health centre to take part in some actions away from that particular position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: No. Not while I was there. We spent that time next to the health centre. All that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did the number of men increase? What was -- how did the things stand later on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Yes. In time, the number of soldiers grew and I believe it reached 70, 80, that is my guess. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did the unit change its name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Yes, it did. It came to be called Vinko Skrobo ATG.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did this unit link up with some other units in the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
