utterances.text: I think that we were part of the town command, that our command was the town command, that is only an assumption because I was just a foot soldier. I do not really know but it is my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: You tell us you were a foot soldier. What does it mean to be a foot soldier in Vinko Skrobo unit? What are the tasks of a foot soldier? Tell us what a foot soldier's day looked like.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Well, it meant that you had to be on duty, that is shifts which lasted eight, sometimes eight, sometimes 12 hours. And we did those shifts on the front line next to the health centre. The shifts lasted eight or 12 hours. And then we would be offer for the next two or three shifts, and then we'd be on duty back again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I will show you a map, or rather a photograph, an aerial photograph, which shows part of the Bulevar, and then I will ask you to look at the photograph and to point at some locations that I will ask you about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Par, please inform us about the number of that photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm so sorry. It is 14.5, the photograph that we've used before whenever we had witnesses who were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Witness, you see this photograph. Is it 14.5? Did I give you the right photograph? No, I'm sorry, I made a mistake, no I gave you 14.4 and yet I want 14.5, so will you please? It's the same thing actually but from a shorter distance. Very good. Now, Witness, do you -- are you familiar with this part of the town? Can you find your way about? Do you know what we see in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with it. We see the front line which we guarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now, I will ask you to take the marker and make a circle around the front line that you guarded, that the Vinko Skrobo unit guarded.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: [marks] Shall I -- no. This is be fine. This is the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Uh-huh. I see, this is the front line. Now, which are the facilities inside the circle? This first building, the largest building, what is this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: This is the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I see, the health centre. At that time, did this health centre look as it does on this photograph or differently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: During the war, it was destroyed. It had been set fire to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you show on this photograph where were your positions inside the health centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: They were on the ground floor of these two buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So nobody was in front of them. You were all inside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: But we can see yet another building here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Yes, there is another building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And what was in that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: That building is somewhat away from the front line and that is where we would repose when we were not on the front line. That was the reserve.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Will you point at this building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: [indicates] So this second building is some 50 metres away from the front line itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So put number 1 next to the health centre.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: That is the front line. And put number 2 on the building which housed the reserve.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very good. Now, what does -- there is a mean. What is the difference between the front line and the reserve. What does a soldier who is in the health centre do and what does a soldier who is in this reserve building, number 2, do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: In building number 1, that is on the fronts line, he has to be with a rifle and on the ready, that is ready to engage in fighting in case of an attack. Building number 2 which is not directly on the front line which and which is protected by the buildings in front of it served for rest so that we could have some coffee there and have a rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So you're a foot soldier. You are on your shift. Where do you go when you're on duty? Where do you pass through? Show us where and what would you do that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: We'd come here. We'd take this path between the buildings in this direction as I'm pointing, like this. Going through gardens and yards.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And on the other side of the Bulevar is the BH Army and their snipers. Do you have any protection. How do you pass through? How are you protected from their fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: No. We moved between the buildings. We tried to take that way so as not to be exposed to the buildings which were on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So you arrived there on duty and how many of you are in the health centre, how many of you are on the reserve, on standby?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Well, ten or 15 of us come and on the front line, itself, there are seven or eight of us, thereabouts, and the rest are on standby.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So what happens during the day? Is there fighting all the time? Gunfire? Action? What does an ordinary day look like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Well, it depended, really. At times, several days would pass by without any conflict, without a single bullet being fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Are you well-protected here when you are there? How is it fortified? What is the -- what kind of shelter do you have? Are you at risk whilst you are there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Well, of course there is. It is a front line and there are snipers on both sides so you have to take care.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: But what kind of protection, what kind of a shield did you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Well, we had in windows, we had sandbags.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Where? In this first building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: In the first building on the ground floor of the first building, in the windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Were there any other sand bags?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Yes, across this street here. So between this building there and this one building. So across the street, there was -- there were sandbags.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Anything else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Yes, there were the hedge hogs, which were antitank barriers and there was also a cord drawn between these two buildings and some carpets were suspended there so you could not see people on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: If it is not difficult for you will you please take the marker and indicate the sand bag, this row of sandbags and possibly the hedge hogs and this cord?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: This is where the sand bags were. This here. And the hedge hogs were in front of it, like this. And the cord was, I think, drawn somewhere between these two buildings, I believe and there were carpets hanging from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So this is the front line. And this building with the reserves, was it safe or was it much safer than the -- in the buildings number 1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Well, in relation to this front line buildings, of course it was quite safe although of course any building in the town could be hit by a shell or something and it was not that far from the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now, apart from this front line, did you have a command somewhere? Where was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Our command was some ten minutes on foot from the front line, west ward, on Kalemova Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And what did the command do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Well, you could go there, have a coffee, have a chat, nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: But you personally, did you spend most of your time at the front line or in the command building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I was at the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now, you've told us what kind of protection you had, the front line, these carpets and all that. Was it all in place when you joined the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Yes, it was all in place already, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you ever see a prisoner of war participate in building these protective devices, working there at the front line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now, you tell us, these are ordinary days, sometimes there is gunfire, sometimes there isn't. Do you remember a day when there was quite a lots of gunfire, and that was the 17th of September, 1993, when allegedly a tank also took part in an action exactly there, right next to that front line, at the health centre. Were you there on that particular day and do you have any recollection of that action?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Yes. I remember it. I was at the front line that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Will you describe to us the developments that day? Where were you? Will you show us first on the map and will you mark it? Where were you that day? And tell us briefly what kind of an action was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I was in the building marked 1, on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you make a small circle to indicate where exactly were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Here exactly, in the middle of this white building, on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And what happened then? At about what time did you get there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: All I know is that it was before noon. I can't give you the exact hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption, Mr. President. Just an observation. I'm not -- I don't intend to object to this testimony because it's obviously central. I would note, however, that if one reads the witness summary that's been provided in respect of this witness, and compares it to what I think we are about to hear, the Trial Chamber may conclude that the Prosecution is not in a position to really cross-examine as to the events of 17 September, certainly not today. We've had no indication whatsoever that this incident was going to be explored in such detail with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Par, from the submissions of your documents, we see only a very few lines on the summary of this -- of the testimony of this witness. You did not indicate the 17th incident. But of course we know that this witness said that he was present at the front line at that time. It was very essential information that we would like to hear. Can you give us an explanation about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Mr. President. I do not have the summary before me because -- so I don't know all the things that I've omitted. But I think that simply this Prosecution's objection is groundless. If in a summary I describe that we have a soldier who was a member of the Vinko Skrobo ATG, who spent several months with that unit, and the months when this unit was active are -- involve also the 9th of May, 1993 and several months. Now do I have to place a special emphasis on that and tell the Prosecutor he was there on the 17th and not on the 18th? He was there on the I don't know what date? Is he -- of course I didn't do it on purpose. I simply thought it logical if I say that somebody was a soldier of a certain period of time, that naturally I will also be asking him, well, did you see Harmandzic, were you there on the 17th of September? I will ask him about everything that happened during his service there. And that is the only reason why that is not in the summary. There are no ruses or any particular tactics involved there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage, could I ask you how long are you going to take for your direct examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, another 20, 15, 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank very much. Mr. Stringer, I don't think you could finish your cross-examination today since we only have 45 minutes this morning. You may continue your cross-examination tomorrow morning while this afternoon or this evening you could prepare all the incidents concerning the 17th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Par, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So let's go back to the 17th of September. You've drawn this little circle to show us where you were then. Now, tell us what happened from that moment when you arrived in building number 1 on? When did this action start? How long did it take? And what did it look like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: It started in the morning. We were planning to attack and cross to the other side, and a tank came to support us. However, that tank didn't prove of much use unfortunately. That tank reached those obstacles, fired perhaps two or maybe three shells, and then went, turned around and went to the building that I've marked with number 1. Its driver refused to fire any more shots and his explanation was that a sniper had hit his optical sights on the tank. I don't know whether it is true or not. That is what he told us. So he stayed behind the building throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Well, there was some exchange of -- there was quite a fierce, quite an intensive exchange of fire, and I heard that some of the guys from the unit that was to the right of us had got killed, and that is why we broke off and stopped the action.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long did it take?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Well, an hour or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you or soldiers who were with you leave the building number 1 towards the Bulevar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And where -- how far did they get to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: They reached as far as a wall in front of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did they ever reach the Bulevar or did they remain behind that wall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I don't know. Some may have been able to run across quickly and then return.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Were there any soldiers next to that tank? Did you see that in that operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Did I see soldiers? No. I saw the tank but I can promise you that there were no soldiers next to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Tell me, on that day, and on that front line, were there any prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: If you didn't see them, did you maybe hear stories about prisoners of war being used on that day as human shields?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Human shields? The only thing I heard about that was when I spoke to some lawyers. That's the only time I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: One part of the indictment alleges that there were some prisoners of war with wooden rifles next to that tank.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: What human shield are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: My question is did you ever see prisoners of war or did you hear that on that day, in your unit, prisoners of war were used as human shields and that they were walking by that tank with a wooden rifles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: If there had been, they had been there, I would have seen them. It's nonsense. There were no people close to that tank. The only person who can say something like that is the person who doesn't know the first thing about the army. Why would there be people next to the tank?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Why do you think that from the military point of view this is nonsense?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: A human shield cannot be used to protect a tank. Everybody in the army can tell you that. They would be killed that very second. I was injured on the front line because I was careless just for a tiny brief second. You can still see the scar on my face so I know exactly what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: We can go back to that later to that injury. We are now talking about prisoners of war. Were there prisoners of war in your unit at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: We can call them differently but if you are using that term, then, okay, let's say that there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Where did they come from? Were they captured by the unit or did they come from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I believe -- I assume that they were brought from the Heliodrom but that's just my guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you see them in the unit? If you did, where did you see them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: They would come to the base and a few of them were in this building for the reserves, and they were there in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you ever see them on the front line in the object marked 1 or next to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: No, I didn't see them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: When they were in the base or in the number 2 building, were they exposed to the enemy fire? Were their lives at any risk or danger?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: That was not the front line so one couldn't say that they lives were endangered or their lives were endangered in so far as the lives of the civilians on the right bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: What did they do in the unit? Slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I usually see them working with the cars. They were repairing some cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: How did the soldiers treat them? Were they harassed by the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I never, and I repeat never, saw any of our soldiers harass any of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Where did they eat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: They ate in the same restaurant as we.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Which restaurant was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: The name of the restaurant is Hladovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did they receive any visits? Were they enabled to contact their families?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them went home almost every evening, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you see any of the prisoners being injured or killed while they were with your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: How did Stela treat them? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I -- to my mind, he treated them correctly. I never saw him doing anything bad to any of the prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of somebody called Nenad Harmandzic, who was a prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of a person called Halil Ajanic, Lopata, who may have been a prisoner of war as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard of him but it is the first time that I hear that he was a prisoner of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you personally ever see Halil Ajanic in your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: He came once and he spoke with Stela. I heard that there had been an accident involving his child.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: What did you hear about that accident? What kind of an accident was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: This Halil, Lopata, had a son who was six or seven years of age, and this kid would frequently come to our unit. I don't know why. Maybe some of our soldiers gave him cookies or sweets. And once I heard there had been an accident, that the kid was killed by a grenade in the apartment of some German guy. And I know that Stela immediately chased that German guy away and told me -- told him never to return again, and I believe that the police saw him out of the town. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: About this Halil Ajanic. What kind after person is he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I knew him before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Is he an alcoholic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Yes, he's known as an alcoholic but also he's very prone to all sorts of crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: How do you know that, that he is prone to crime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Before the war, he worked in the warehouse of a construction materials. That was during the socialist time. There was a lack of building material and he smuggled that from his warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Let's move on to another topic. My question is: Did your unit take part in the expulsion of Muslims from the western part of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: As far as I know, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you personally ever participate in anybody's eviction from their apartment, in anybody's expulsion, or do you know any of your colleagues who may have done that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I personally never expelled anybody. Our unit as such never expelled anybody. However, the truth is that there were all sorts of rumours circulating around the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: What rumours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: The town on both sides was full of refugees from all over the place, from Konjic, from Sarajevo. There were a lot more refugees than the locals. There were ten refugees to one local inhabitant. And in such a difficult situation, these people probably resorted to all sorts of means. Some of them even illegal. And one of the easiest way for them to solve the problem of accommodation was to expel a Muslim inhabitant of that apartment and to assign that act to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Why to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Because we were the best-known unit in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: What you're saying now, is that what you think or what you know or you have some experience to base that on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I know of a case when a couple of guys who did not belong to our unit put stockings on their heads so nobody could recognise them, and they stole people's cars. And they referred to each other as Stela and Brada. Later on, people went to the police and reported Stela as the perpetrator of the car theft. Stela, as far as I know, told the police that on that incriminated day, he was not even in Mostar, that he was in Split but he himself realised that he would have to look for these people himself because this went too far. War was nonsense as such and it was even compounded by people, by things being ascribed to Stela, although he didn't do them. And I know that eventually he found these two guys. I assume that he turned them over to the police. I don't know. But I heard that before that, he gave them a good beating.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: They were not members of your unit, were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And in conclusion, can you please tell us something about Stela as a commander? What was his treatments of his soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: The only reason why I joined his unit is because I respected him. He did not use military discipline. He was always amicable. He was always friendly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: What was his relationship with other commanders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: It was good and correct relationship from what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: What was his treatment of Muslims, civilians, from the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I believe that the treatment was correct, and I also know of a number of people whom he helped.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And one more thing. Let me ask you, before I forget. You mentioned that you were injured on the front line. In very brief lines, can you please tell us how were you injured and can we please have this medical certificate on the certificate? I don't wish to tender that into evidence. I just want this to be used as a reminder for the witness. I received that from you yesterday. Can you just briefly tell us how were you injured and what consequences did you suffer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we are in the open session. So Mr. Usher don't put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Don't put it on the ELMO. Look at it, don't read your name. What date was that when you were admitted, as can be seen in this medical report? Why were you admitted? How were you injured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I was injured on the 12th of July, 1993. I was injured in the following way. I was in the bunker.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So can we show that on the map, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I was in the building number 1 on the ground floor, left to the centre. So it is the left room on -- in this photo. I made a mistake. I was moving by the opening in the bunker. And the only thing that the sharp shooter could see was my shadow. But that was enough for him to take a shot, to pierce the sand bag, because he shot from a rather close range. And the bullet hit the -- my rifle, the frame of my rifle, which burst into pieces, and I suffered shrapnel injuries all over the body. I still have a large shrapnel in my head and a lot of smaller ones all over the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. Your Honours, this completes my examination-in-chief. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Can I just give the number to this exhibit, the one just marked by the witness, 14.5, I think that should be D2/46, no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Madam Registrar, we could deal with it during the proceedings of admitting those documents into the evidence. Now let the Prosecutor conduct the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: My name is Doug Stringer. I'm going to ask you some questions on behalf of the Prosecution. The first couple of questions I want to ask you about is you testified in your direct examination about the change of the name of Mr. Martinovic's unit and in connection with that issue, I want to ask the Registrar to show you two exhibits, 577 and 520.1. While those are coming, Mr. Witness, I'll just make a couple of comments. I don't expect you to recognise yourself either of these documents, but I do want to use these as a basis on which to ask you a question or two. The first one is Exhibit 577, and take a moment to look it over. I'm interested in the very last paragraph on this document. This is a document or a report dated the 25th of August, 1993, and my question, sir, is whether, drawing your attention to the last paragraph, whether this document, the indication here corresponds to your own testimony, that is that the name of the unit changed from Mrmak ATG to the new name of Vinko Skrobo ATG, approximately latter July or the early part of August? Would that be consistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: It may be so but I cannot be sure of the day when that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object to such a presentation of exhibits to the witness, because I believe that this is just an attempt to tender into evidence the documents which have not been admitted so far. This is an official record which is negative [As interpreted] By its contents for this Defence. The Trial Chamber has refused the -- to admit this document into evidence and now an attempt is being made to use just one sentence out of the context, which is not even important for the document, to again have this document admitted, and the witness is abused in this way. So my objection would consist of the following: the way the documents which have nothing to do with the testimony are presented to the witness consist the abuse of the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Par, are you talking about document P577 or some other document? If you're talking about document P577 I have to say that this document has already been admitted and we also believe that the last paragraph of this document is relevant to the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is the document that I'm talking about, Mr. President. I can see that it has been admitted but my objection stands. I believe that such a presentation of an exhibit with just one sentence outside of the context being presented to the witness, is a forceful way of presenting something to the Trial Chamber. I believe still that the witness is being abused in this way because the contents of the document, the entire document, have nothing to do with the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: On this very point, I agree with you, that this witness is entitled to read the whole document and then the Prosecution could ask some questions concerning with one sentence or paragraph. But at the same time, I have to remind you, Mr. Par, do not talk about the documents while we still have this witness giving the testimony. You have the full right to do it at a later stage. Mr. Stringer, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, if you need to take another moment or so to read the document, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to briefly respond. I must reject the assertion that I'm abusing the witness. I think it's offensive to be accused of such a thing in the presence of the witness when I'm just leading off on a cross-examination. Secondly, Mr. Par, my learned friend, led evidence about the change of the name of this unit. He did not give us a point in time in which that is alleged to have occurred. I have documents at hand which may assist the Trial Chamber and all of us in knowing when that change in the name occurred, more or less, and I think I'm in a position and I think it is proper to ask the witness whether this time frame indicated on this document and the next document I intend to show him are roughly consistent with his own recollection about the time frame involved. That's all I'm trying to do is get this attached to a particular period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll take note of what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So witness, again, and so you know, and the Trial Chamber knows, the matters that are discussed in the first three paragraphs or so are not of interest to me and they are not of relevance to this case. What is of interest to me is the last part which indicates that some 15 to 20 days ago the Mrmak ATG got a new name and now goes by the name of Vinko Skrobo ATG. Now, again, this document is dated 25th of August, 1993, so I know you can't remember the exact day but I'm simply asking you: Is the rough time frame, early August, generally consistent with your own recollection of the time when the name of the unit changed from Mrmak to Vinko Skrobo? That's all I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I can only repeat that I cannot give you a precise answer. My very big concern was how to save my life at the time, not to try and remember the exact dates when things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll ask you to now take a look at the next exhibit, which is 520.1. Take a moment to read that document, and after we are finished I'm going to draw your attention to the handwritten part that's in the upper, right-hand corner of the document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Okay. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is a document dated the 14th of July, 1993, which I note is only about two days after you were injured on the front line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me look at the date. I don't see a date here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In the handwritten part, I'm sorry, the handwritten note.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Yes. Now I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then you see the hand written note indicating again that the stamp for the unit need not be made because the name had been changed. Are you able to recall whether the name had changed from Mrmak to Vinko Skrobo before or after the time you were injured, which is essentially the same time that this document was made?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask it a different way. Was the unit that you were a member of called the Vinko Skrobo on the day you were injured or was it called the Mrmak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you. I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In any event, sir, it's your testimony that the name of the unit was changed to Mrmak and Vinko Skrobo at some point during the summer of 1993? Is that a fair estimation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In the time that we have left today, sir, I'd like to ask you a few questions about the HOS, which you've testified about in your direct examination. And if I understand correctly, sir, correct me if I'm wrong, you were in Croatia working in Croatia in the spring of 1992, and it was in Croatia that you actually joined the HOS. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Yes. I mean to join this HOS, that was the procedure. One had to become a member of a political party, which is called HSP. So it was in Croatia that I did it in a place called Vrgorac and then with their membership card they sent me to their headquarters, which was in Ljubuski in B and H, but it is quite near the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: HOS in Croatia had a connection or a link to HOS in Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I suppose so. I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: HOS in addition to being -- having a political aspect to it, also had a military aspect to as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Paraga the leader of the HOS in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you ever meet him in Zagreb before you came down to Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The HOS in Ljubuski, I think you testified, was composed of Croats and Muslims fighting together against the Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the leader of the HOS in Ljubuski at that time was a man by the name of Blaz Kraljevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And again I think we are talking about the period of time roughly April of 1992, before the liberation of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, in June of 1992, when you fought as part of the operation which led to the liberation of Mostar, where exactly were you positioned as a member of Mr. Martinovic's HOS unit? Where were you deployed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: There was only one unit in the town, and I was just a foot soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the HOS unit that was in Mostar, there were HVO units that were also involved in this operation against the Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So at that time you had actually two different military organisations which were fighting against the Serbs. You had the HVO on one hand, you had the HOS on the other hand, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: After the liberation of Mostar in 1992, and perhaps even before, did a certain degree of rivalry or competition surface between the HVO and the HOS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: It began to happen after Mostar was liberated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And that was because there was a struggle as to which of these two organisations was going to take control of Mostar. Isn't that the basis of the dispute?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I guess so but I'm a foot soldier and for me, this is already -- now, I can only make some assumptions. I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then in August of 1992, Blaz Kraljevic was assassinated in the region out side of Mostar toward Siroki Brijeg; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I'm sure it's a simplification but after his death, then, the HOS, the HOS essentially dissolved or fell apart in Bosnia and Herzegovina and many members of HOS units then moved over into the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Including yourself and also Mr. Martinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you have knowledge of the different goals or objectives of HOS as opposed to HVO, different policies of those two organisations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I have to repeat it once again that I am just an ordinary foot soldier. These questions are way above me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know a gentleman whose -- let me back up, I'm sorry, in the few minutes we have left today. You testified, I believe, on your direct, that the commander of the ATG Vinko Skrobo was Vinko Martinovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You indicated that the unit was divided into four groups, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did each of those four groups have someone who was the leader or the commander, if you will?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was Ernest Takac one of those?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was he a correct soldier, in your view?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: As far as I know him, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And was a man named Dubi, Mr. Pehar, was he also a leader of one of the groups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: He was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was he a correct soldier, in your view?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were those two persons involved in extensive evictions of Muslims throughout West Mostar during the time that you were a member of the Vinko Skrobo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You don't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I don't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If I put it to you sir, this those two individuals, together with Mr. Martinovic, were personally involved in evicting Muslims from West Mostar, that would be a revelation to you, something you never knew before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: It would, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: When you were not on your shift on the front line, where did you spend your time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: In the flat with my parents, that is my mother. She was the only one there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And that's in the area of West Mostar that you indicated previously?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know a person or did you hear of a person named Ivan Andabak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I've heard about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know of a person named Romeo Blazevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I've heard about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was he associated with the ATG Vinko Skrobo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Who gave you your orders directly, when you received orders, from whom did they come?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: From my immediate superior. That is the group commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And who was your group commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Bogo Peric.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll ask that the witness be shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Before we do that let me ask you a question. It may speed things along. Are you aware of an incident in August, 1993, when Mr. Takac was involved in an informal exchange of prisoners, one from the west side and one from the east side? The name of the prisoner was Mujanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: I really knew nothing about it. This is the first time I hear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was it possible for informal cease-fires to be called by which persons could be passed across the confrontation line as part of an informally arranged exchange?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: That could be it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about that yourself? Did you see any of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see it, but -- so I can again make some assumptions. Perhaps it could happen somewhere. It didn't happen during my shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were injured on the 12th of July, 1993. How much it did that result in your being off of the front line for a period of time while you healed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Yes. I was absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And how long were you absent from the front line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: Ten days perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were you in the hospital during that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP
utterances.text: The first day, the day of the wounding, and then I came for checkups.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can break at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. It is time. Witness, as I did to any other witnesses that we have to keep you here for another day, you have to remember that you are still under the oath so during your stay in The Hague, do not talk to anybody about your testimony and do not let anybody talk to you about it. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will see you in the morning, 9.00, in the same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: 1.45 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 5th day of September, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
